clinicalPearls: Normal arterial CO2 (Paco2) sits between roughly 37 and 43 mmHg at sea level; all ventilatory disorders manifest as an abnormal Paco2 (Harrison 22e p.2273).

Because Paco2 is governed by Paco2 = k(VCO2)/VA, every disturbance reflects altered CO2 production, minute ventilation, or dead-space fraction; a patient can breathe rapidly with a high minute ventilation yet still hypoventilate at the alveolar level if dead space is increased (Harrison 22e p.2273).

Respiratory rhythm is generated in the brainstem (dorsal respiratory group and ventral respiratory column); the pre-Botzinger complex within the VRC is critical for inspiration, and its lesioning abolishes breathing entirely (Harrison 22e p.2273).
Normal sleep brings an attenuated response to hypercapnia and hypoxemia, producing mild nocturnal hypoventilation that corrects on awakening (Harrison 22e p.2273).

New-onset orthopnea is one of the earliest signs of reduced diaphragmatic force generation; 'paradoxical breathing' (abdomen moving inward on deep inspiration while supine) signals significant diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis (Harrison 22e p.2274).

Chronic hypoventilation follows a characteristic sequence: an asymptomatic stage with normal daytime gases, then nocturnal hypoventilation appearing first in REM then non-REM sleep, then falling vital capacity, and finally daytime hypercapnia (Harrison 22e p.2274).

The shared hallmark of all alveolar hypoventilation syndromes is a rise in alveolar and arterial Pco2 with a compensatory increase in plasma bicarbonate; the rising Paco2 displaces alveolar oxygen and commonly causes hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2274).

Chronic hypoxemia from hypoventilation can drive secondary erythrocytosis, and the combination of chronic hypoxemia and hypercapnia can cause pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy, and right heart failure (Harrison 22e p.2274).

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) requires BMI >=30 kg/m2 plus chronic daytime hypoventilation (Paco2 >=45 mmHg) with no other explanation; obstructive sleep apnea coexists in nearly 90% of cases, with about 70% having severe OSA (Harrison 22e p.2275).

In OHS, the depressed ventilatory responsiveness appears to be a consequence rather than a primary cause, since central drive often improves once sleep-disordered breathing is treated without weight change (Harrison 22e p.2276).

Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (Ondine's curse, CCHS) is linked to PHOX2b gene abnormalities; affected patients lack ventilatory responses to hypoxia/hypercapnia, have mild waking hypercapnia, markedly elevated Paco2 in non-REM sleep, yet can paradoxically normalize Paco2 during exercise and REM sleep (Harrison 22e p.2276).

In chronic hyperventilation, anxiety/panic are not synonymous with the condition; sustaining hypocapnia needs only about a 10% increase in alveolar ventilation, achievable through subtle pattern changes such as occasional sigh breaths or frequent yawning (Harrison 22e p.2277).
harrison.pathophysiology: Adequate ventilation depends on a balance between respiratory drive and neuromuscular strength on one side and the elastic plus resistive loads of the respiratory system on the other. Reduced drive, impaired neuromuscular competence, or a markedly increased load lowers effective minute ventilation and produces hypercapnia; conversely, normal muscle strength combined with excessive drive yields hyperventilation and hypocapnia. Diseases reducing minute ventilation or increasing dead space fall into four broad categories: parenchymal lung/chest wall disease, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease, and respiratory drive disorders. 'Pump failure' encompasses disorders of drive, neural pathways, the neuromuscular junction, and muscle. In OHS the mechanism is multifactorial, combining OSA, increased work of breathing, respiratory muscle impairment against an excess-adiposity load, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and blunted central responsiveness to hypoxemia and hypercapnia. Chronic hyperventilation is conceptualized as having initiating and sustaining factors, with an initial event dropping Paco2 toward ~20 mmHg and resultant symptoms perpetuating overbreathing (Harrison 22e p.2273-2277).
additionalDifferentials: Parenchymal lung disease (obstructive such as COPD; restrictive such as interstitial lung disease; atelectasis; pulmonary embolus)
Chest wall disorders (kyphoscoliosis, obesity, abdominal distention/ascites)
Neuromuscular disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, phrenic nerve injury, spinal cord lesion, myopathy, muscular dystrophy)
Depressed respiratory drive (narcotic/sedative use, brainstem stroke, hypothyroidism, primary alveolar hypoventilation)
Brainstem structural lesions of the pons or medulla (stroke, tumor)
infectionMimics: Recurrent pneumonia from ineffective cough in neuromuscular disease can mimic or precipitate acute respiratory deterioration
nonInfectiousMimics: Anxiety disorders and panic attacks (overlap with but are not equivalent to chronic hyperventilation)
Mild asthma producing respiratory alkalosis (must be excluded before diagnosing chronic hyperventilation)
Diabetic ketoacidosis presenting as acute hyperventilation
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gas (the diagnostic hallmark): Paco2 >=45 mmHg defines hypoventilation; venous blood gas is an alternative, recognizing venous Pco2 runs a few points higher than arterial

Serum bicarbonate (total CO2) as a sensitive but nonspecific screen: a level <27 mmol/L with normal renal function makes hypoventilation very unlikely, while >=27 mmol/L should prompt Paco2 measurement
Chest x-ray and/or CT to identify lung/chest wall disease
Pulmonary function testing including seated-versus-supine FVC (a 15-25% supine drop suggests diaphragmatic weakness) plus maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures
Polysomnography to demonstrate nocturnal hypercapnia, central versus obstructive apneas/hypopneas, and to screen for OSA
Brain CT or MRI to detect pontine/medullary structural lesions
OSA screening tools (Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Berlin Questionnaire, STOP-Bang) recognizing their limited sensitivity/specificity
Genetic testing for PHOX2b abnormalities in suspected congenital central hypoventilation syndrome
redFlags: Paradoxical (abdominal) breathing while supine indicating significant diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis
New-onset orthopnea heralding reduced respiratory muscle force in neuromuscular disease
Progressive 15-25% supine fall in FVC signaling impending chronic respiratory failure
Daytime hypercapnia developing on top of established nocturnal hypoventilation
Signs of secondary erythrocytosis, pulmonary hypertension, or right heart failure from chronic hypoxemia/hypercapnia
harrison.prognosis: Chronic hypercapnia in COPD marks more advanced disease and carries worse survival than in equally severe normocapnic patients. Documented daytime hypercapnia treated with nocturnal noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation is associated with improved daytime gas exchange, prolonged survival, and better health-related quality of life. In OHS with severe OSA, both CPAP and NIPPV improve long-term Paco2/bicarbonate and reduce cardiovascular and overall mortality. Progressive neuromuscular disease tends to advance from sleep-only to round-the-clock ventilatory support need, though modern home ventilation can delay tracheostomy and institutionalization (Harrison 22e p.2275-2276).
pitfalls: Equating high minute ventilation with adequate alveolar ventilation: increased dead space can produce alveolar hypoventilation despite rapid breathing (Harrison 22e p.2273).
Diagnosing primary respiratory drive disorder without excluding far more common secondary causes such as sedatives, chronic narcotics, and significant hypothyroidism (Harrison 22e p.2275).

Misattributing chronic hyperventilation symptoms to cardiopulmonary disease and failing to exclude acute causes (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis, mild asthma) before labeling it chronic (Harrison 22e p.2276-2277).
Overlooking that supplemental oxygen, even at low concentrations, can worsen hypercapnia in some hypoventilating patients (Harrison 22e p.2276).
Failing to recognize that a serum bicarbonate elevated out of proportion to chronic respiratory acidosis (excess metabolic alkalosis) can itself aggravate hypoventilation (Harrison 22e p.2276).
harrison.severityClassification: Diagnostic thresholds rather than a formal grading scale: hypoventilation is defined by Paco2 >=45 mmHg; OHS requires BMI >=30 kg/m2 plus Paco2 >=45 mmHg without another cause; severe OSA is an apnea-hypopnea index >30 events/h; stable chronic hypercapnic COPD considered for home high-intensity ventilation typically has Paco2 >52 mmHg with normal pH (Harrison 22e p.2275-2276).
management: Nocturnal non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation is the mainstay for chronic hypoventilation and obesity hypoventilation syndrome
Pursue weight loss (including bariatric measures) and treat coexisting obstructive sleep apnoea with CPAP in obesity hypoventilation
Treat the underlying disorder, whether neuromuscular disease, chest-wall disease, or a respiratory drive disorder
Use supplemental oxygen cautiously as an adjunct to avoid suppressing residual respiratory drive, and avoid sedatives that depress ventilation
Monitor progression with serial vital capacity, blood gases, and polysomnography
Escalate to tracheostomy and long-term ventilation when non-invasive support fails or bulbar and respiratory muscle failure advances
Provide vaccination and prompt treatment of respiratory infections
Coordinate care through a respiratory and, in neuromuscular disease, neurology multidisciplinary team
